lines: Prompted by the new Elizabeth Holmes documentary, Ted Seides argues that allocators' search for certainty often yields reassurance rather than truth, and that more transparency can add confusion instead of clarity.
He says manager meetings, especially after underperformance, become a ritual in which managers offer comforting narratives and project confidence because that is what the questions reward.

Since market noise makes precise attribution of cause and effect nearly impossible, he suggests judging managers by temperament, accountability and consistency under pressure rather than by their literal explanations.
His fix: ask falsifiability questions, such as what would change their mind or where the process could fail, and recognize how the allocator's own expectations shape the answers they get.
podcast: Capital Allocators – Inside the Institutional Investment Industry
title: WTT: You Can't See Everything
